How Xi Sees a Weakened Trump

Voters dealt U.S. President Donald Trump a crushing rebuke in the Nov. 3 midterm elections, with Republicans losing control of both chambers of Congress. As Trump meets once again with Xi Jinping this week, how will the Chinese leader now view a weakened U.S. president?

It has been revealed that I believe Xi will not fundamentally change his personal assessment of Trump. But he is reassessing Trump’s ability to shape U.S.-China relations over the next two years—and the extent to which the two leaders can deliver on the new framework for bilateral relations they agreed on this year. Beijing may come to see Trump as a president who remains willing to negotiate on a personal level but is becoming less capable of delivering on major political commitments.

Voters dealt U.S. President Donald Trump a crushing rebuke in the Nov. 3 midterm elections, with Republicans losing control of both chambers of Congress. As Trump meets once again with Xi Jinping this week, how will the Chinese leader now view a weakened U.S. president?

I believe Xi will not fundamentally change his personal assessment of Trump. But he is reassessing Trump’s ability to shape U.S.-China relations over the next two years—and the extent to which the two leaders can deliver on the upcoming framework for bilateral relations they agreed on this year. Beijing may come to see Trump as a president who remains willing to negotiate on a personal level but is becoming less capable of delivering on major political commitments.

This matters because both Xi and Trump place considerable importance on personal diplomacy between heads of state. Trump visited China in May, and Xi traveled to the United States in September. During those meetings, according to the Chinese readout, they agreed to establish a latest framework for bilateral relations: a “constructive and strategically stable relationship based on respect, fairness, and reciprocity.” Xi also called for a relationship characterized by “cooperation as the priority, managed competition, controlled differences, and the prospect of peace.”.

Trump, for his part, repeatedly emphasized his good personal relationship with Xi and expressed confidence that U.S.-China relations could succeed under their leadership.

Sources indicate that despite their very different political backgrounds and governing philosophies, Xi and Trump, who have both sought to expand their own authority at home, share a belief that strong leaders can play a decisive role in national decision-making. Beijing routinely emphasizes the strategic importance of diplomacy conducted by heads of state. Trump, meanwhile, distrusts the traditional foreign-policy bureaucracy and prefers to negotiate deals directly with other leaders. Both seem to believe that once leaders reach an understanding, many complicated problems between their countries can be resolved.

But there is a fundamental difference between them. Xi’s autocratic status allows him to translate his personal diplomatic preferences into Chinese government policy. Trump, despite his unusually personal approach to presidential decision-making, cannot entirely circumvent Congress, the judiciary, or other domestic political forces—especially after the recent midterm results.

That difference was less visible when Republicans controlled both the White House and Congress. After returning to office, Trump enjoyed considerable authority within the Republican Party, while a supine Congress offered little effective resistance to his policies, even when pro-Ukrainian Republicans objected to his attempts to cozy up to Russian President Vladimir Putin. Xi had reason to believe that maintaining a stable personal relationship with Trump could help stabilize Washington’s China policy and perhaps even facilitate adjustments to U.S. positions on sensitive challenges through direct negotiations between the two leaders.

It has been revealed that the midterms have changed that. With Democrats controlling Congress, Trump retains substantial authority over foreign affairs, but major agreements he reaches with Xi will face greater congressional scrutiny and potential challenges. On Taiwan and advanced technology in particular, especially after the Jensen Huang scandal, Democrats are not necessarily more accommodating toward China than Republicans. If Trump attempts to make significant concessions to Beijing in these areas, Democrats could use hearings, investigations, budgetary powers, and legislation to obstruct him—and turn any such concessions into political ammunition.

Recent findings suggest that for Trump, however, the more difficult constraint may come from his own party’s political interests. He cannot run for president again, however much he wants to, but Republicans must defend the White House and seek to regain Congress in 2028. If Democrats portray a Trump-Xi agreement as sacrificing Taiwan’s security or undermining America’s technological advantage, Republican candidates will face an uncomfortable choice. Supporting Trump could expose them to accusations of being soft on China; opposing him could alienate MAGA voters. Trump may be willing to disregard Democratic criticism, but he cannot entirely ignore his party’s electoral prospects or his own political legacy.

Recent findings suggest that this creates a paradox. Having lost his congressional majority, Trump may have a stronger incentive to demonstrate his leadership through foreign-policy achievements, making him more eager to reach a major agreement with Xi. Yet the greater his need to present such an agreement as a victory for the United States, the less room he has to appear to be making concessions to China. His weakened political position increases his incentive to strike a deal while simultaneously narrowing the concessions he can offer.

It has been revealed that xi is likely to recognize this. Rather than downgrading the importance of his personal relationship with Trump, he may become even more determined to preserve that direct channel of communication. Compared with Democratic politicians, Trump remains more inclined to approach U.S.-China relations transactionally and more willing to adjust specific policies according to his own judgment. From Chinese leaders’ perspective, he remains someone they can deal with—but they may no longer trust his ability to deliver. He remains a president worth negotiating with.

Beijing set the language after the Trump-Xi meeting in September, with little pushback from the White House. From Beijing’s perspective, the framework represents more than an effort to move beyond the intense trade confrontation of recent years. It also signals, in China’s interpretation, that Washington is beginning to accept China as an equal strategic power and is willing to keep bilateral competition within certain limits. Beijing clearly hopes that the principles of “respect” and “strategic stability” will extend to issues it considers central to its interests, particularly Taiwan and technology.

Yet Trump’s acceptance of this diplomatic language does not mean the entire U.S. political system is on board. Trump himself may well not understand the implications of the Chinese language. For Washington, strategic stability is more about managing conflict, protecting U.S. interests, and preserving competitive advantages.

The Chinese Foreign Ministry’s response to the results of the U.S. midterms offers an indication of Beijing’s approach. Rather than commenting on Trump’s political defeat, its spokesperson emphasized China’s willingness to continue implementing the understandings reached by the two presidents and to advance their constructive, strategically stable relationship.

Sources indicate that xi is unlikely to repudiate diplomatic achievements in which he has invested substantial political capital simply because of a U.S. midterm election. On the contrary, he has good reason to reaffirm the framework and invoke it when pressing Washington to honor the understandings reached between the two leaders.

Industry observers note that but I suspect that the more Beijing emphasizes the framework in its diplomatic rhetoric, the more cautious it will become in practice. This brings us to a second question: How does Xi interpret U.S. politics itself?

Industry observers note that when Trump won reelection in 2024, Republicans also captured both chambers of Congress, and the media was eager to trumpet a latest era of dominant Trumpism. Just two years later, Democrats have won their biggest victory in generations. This sharp reversal may reinforce Xi’s perception that U.S. politics lacks stability and continuity.

Yet Xi would be making a mistake if he interpreted U.S. political divisions as evidence that China now enjoys a greater strategic opportunity. In U.S. politics, the two parties may fight bitterly over domestic issues and presidential authority while maintaining considerable agreement on strategic competition with China.

I expect Beijing to gradually shift the emphasis of its U.S. policy over the next two years. It will continue to maintain Xi’s personal relationship with Trump, seek to implement existing agreements, and avoid another serious confrontation over trade or security. At the same time, it will lower its expectations that leader-to-leader diplomacy can fundamentally redirect U.S.-China relations. Instead, Beijing will accelerate attempts to reduce China’s vulnerability to shifts in U.S. policy during a prolonged period of strategic competition.

Sources indicate that such an adjustment would not mean Xi is preparing for an all-out confrontation with the United States. Because Beijing increasingly recognizes that the competition will be prolonged, it has greater reason to avoid a direct clash before the conditions are in its failure. Maintaining basic stability in U.S.-China relations remains a way to buy time for China’s own development.

Industry observers note that the new framework established by Xi and Trump this year is therefore unlikely to be abandoned easily. Beijing still needs it, and so does Trump. But their expectations may increasingly diverge. Xi wants the framework to provide China with long-term strategic stability, while Trump is more likely to see it as a means of managing relations with Beijing and securing diplomatic achievements during the remainder of his presidency.

For Xi, the central lesson of the midterms may be that he can build personal trust with Trump but he cannot entrust the future of U.S.-China relations to Trump alone.

Deng Yuwen is a Chinese writer and scholar.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Heliene, a solar modules manufacturer, and Caelux Corporation, a perovskite solar technology firm, are starting commercial production of their Hybrid-Tandem solar module.

This module combines perovskite glass from Caelux and silicon N-type cells from Heliene, placing two energy generating sources in a single solar panel. Heliene is producing the modules in its plant in Mountain Iron, Minnesota, with first deliveries slated for 2027.

It has been revealed that “One of the advantages of Caelux’s technology is that we can integrate its Energy Producing Glass into our existing manufacturing lines without having to build an entirely newly introduced production setup,” said Martin Pochtaruk, CEO and founder of Heliene. “With both companies manufacturing in the U.S., we’re bringing together two fully domestic supply chains to advance what’s possible with American-made solar, besides the fact that partnering with true friends also makes it fun.”.

The companies are reporting a 27% efficiency from the Hybrid-Tandem module. Heliene and Caelux desiged this module to have a higher power density in a smaller project footprint.

“Heliene is a true leader in U.S. manufacturing, and we share a belief that when we lead the market, our customers win. Together, we’re commercializing ultra-high-efficiency solar modules that will set a upcoming bar for American-made solar,” said Caelux CEO Scott Graybeal.

Sources indicate that heliene will showcase the Hybrid-Tandem module at RE+ in Las Vegas from Nov. 17 to 19, at booth #W16546.

  • These worries are entirely justified; Trump has a track record of cozying up to autocrats and turning his back on democratic allies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that CHARLES KUPCHAN is Professor of International Affairs at Georgetown University and a Senior Fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations. He is the author of Bringing Order to Anarchy: Governing the World to Come.

Sources indicate that in just a few days’ time, U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese leader Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin could be holding a three-way summit on the sidelines of next week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting in Shenzhen, China. According to The Wall Street Journal, Putin floated the idea of a trialogue last month as an opportunity to discuss ending the war in Ukraine. No firm initiative has yet been revealed, but even the prospect of this meeting has provoked widespread consternation. Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski warned against a repeat of the Yalta Conference of 1945, when U.S. President Franklin Roosevelt and British Prime Minister Winston Churchill capitulated to Soviet leader Joseph Stalin’s push for the Soviet Union to dominate Eastern Europe. U.S. Senator Chris Coons posted on X that “there can be no talks about Ukraine’s future without Ukraine at the table, and there can be no real negotiations as long as Trump signals weakness and servitude to Xi and Putin at every opportunity.”.

These worries are entirely justified; Trump has a track record of cozying up to autocrats and turning his back on democratic allies. Should he sit down with Xi and Putin, he must avoid selling out European and Asian partners who will not be at the table. And given the three leaders’ headstrong personalities and competing national interests that pit the United States against what Xi calls a “no limits” partnership between China and Russia, the meeting might ultimately yield little progress on major challenges.

Nevertheless, Trump would be right to join a summit with Xi and Putin. No U.S. president has ever held a trilateral meeting with the leaders of China and Russia, and the proposed talks would break the ice and begin to normalize much-needed dialogue. Authoritarianism is not going away, so autocracies and democracies must learn not only to live comfortably alongside one another but also to work together to tame geopolitical rivalry and tackle global challenges in an interdependent world. Americans will not find it easy to get along with the likes of Russia and China, whose political systems threaten the U.S. commitment to spreading democracy. But Trump is taking a bold step in the right direction by engaging with the heads of the world’s leading autocracies.

According to recent reports, if he meets with Xi and Putin, Trump should aim low and focus on making meaningful, if limited, progress on a small number of core complications that could benefit from a three-way conversation: the flash points of the Korean Peninsula, Ukraine, and Iran, as well as arms control and strategic stability. But even if the summit yields no concrete results, it will nonetheless have been worthwhile. Trump, Xi, and Putin are paving the way for their successors to advance great-power cooperation across ideological lines and stabilize a fragmented world.

I have argued previously, including in a 2021 Foreign Affairs essay with Richard Haass, that a global concert—an informal steering group of great powers modeled on the nineteenth-century Concert of Europe—offers the best hope of curbing geopolitical competition and enabling collective action in a multipolar world. In addition to the United States, China, and Russia, a latest concert would include India, Japan, the European Union, and representatives from Africa, Latin America, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia. Concerts sacrifice representation for efficacy and give only the geopolitically influential states that must be there a seat at the table. They set aside ideological differences and bring democracies and autocracies together to focus on international cooperation. Because concerts eschew binding, enforceable procedures in favor of informal consensus building, they can succeed when formal institutions such as the UN Security Council are paralyzed and when the United States wavers in its commitment to rules-based multilateralism.

But the time has not come for a global concert. Concerts function effectively only when their members are committed to the territorial status quo, are willing to exercise strategic restraint and pursue mutual benefits, and are ready to settle disputes diplomatically. Putin’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine and Xi’s decision to back Russia have, for now, scuttled hopes that the great powers will normalize restraint and the peaceful settlement of disputes. Meanwhile, Trump’s “America first” statecraft shuns joint action and mutual gain in favor of unilateralism.

It has been revealed that yet even though Trump, Xi, and Putin are the wrong leaders at the wrong time to establish a great-power steering group that other major players would eventually join, Trump’s iconoclastic diplomacy sets a useful precedent. His Alaska summit with Putin last year and two summits with Xi this year were admittedly long on pageantry and short on substance. But by taking the controversial step of pursuing joint talks with the two leaders, Trump is widening the diplomatic Overton window and expanding what is politically possible for future U.S. presidents. Avoiding great-power conflict and taming a world in increasing disarray requires the United States to build constructive relations with both China and Russia. Trump deserves credit for starting a trialogue that his successors can carry forward.

If they meet in Shenzhen, Trump, Xi, and Putin should focus on easing tensions at key geopolitical flash points. The Korean Peninsula presents the best opportunity for the three leaders to collaborate. At the UN General Assembly in September, South Korean President Lee Jae-myung laid out an ambitious blueprint for normalizing relations with Pyongyang, including a proposal to replace the peninsula’s 1953 armistice with a “peace regime” that promotes “respect for each other’s systems and acknowledgement of our differences.” As part of that plan, Lee has advocated a phased approach to North Korean denuclearization, with an initial freeze on weapons development followed by gradual reductions in Pyongyang’s arsenal of nuclear weapons and ballistic missiles until the peninsula is denuclearized.

According to recent reports, lee’s bold proposal could bring U.S., Chinese, and Russian interests into alignment. Trump has made it clear that he wants to de-escalate tensions on the Korean Peninsula and is already seeking a meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. Beijing and Moscow are competing for influence over Kim, but both want a stable relationship between North and South Korea, so they might be willing to cooperate on proposals to halt nuclear weapons production and encourage talks between Pyongyang and Seoul. Trump, Xi, and Putin should aim to emerge from their meeting with a plan for advancing Lee’s peace agenda; jointly supporting a freeze on North Korean nuclear weapons development is a good place to start.

Recent findings suggest that the prospects for progress toward ending the war in Ukraine are much dimmer but not nonexistent. Trump should be striving to weaken Russia’s ability to sustain the war, but he has long resisted tightening sanctions on Moscow. He talks up potential business ventures with Russia and, in recent weeks, even struck a deal with Putin to get more Russian diesel into global markets and waived a upcoming round of congressional sanctions against Moscow. Trump evidently cares more about trying to bring down fuel prices than about curbing Russia’s ability to fund its war against Ukraine.

Sources indicate that A summit offers Trump the opportunity to change course and try to convince Xi to restrain Putin. Trump has vowed to bring the war in Ukraine to an end, and the Chinese leader can help him achieve that goal. Xi has enormous leverage over Putin: China backs the Kremlin diplomatically, is the largest buyer of Russian oil and gas, and is the main supplier of dual-use items such as semiconductors and machine tools that are critical to Russian weapons manufacturing.

Industry observers note that xi has played along with Putin’s war against Ukraine so far, presumably because the conflict diverts U.S. attention and resources away from Asia, divides NATO, and allows Xi and Putin to cast themselves as leading a global resistance to Western hegemony. But when Xi and Trump met this May, the leaders agreed to pursue “a constructive relationship of strategic stability” between China and the United States, which Xi could advance by pressing Putin to de-escalate. As more Russians feel the effects of the war, the Kremlin may be newly receptive to such pressure. Ukrainian drone strikes are taking a significant toll on Russia’s oil sector and logistics networks, which means Russian citizens face mounting gas and commodities shortages. Meanwhile, some 35,000 Russian soldiers per month are losing their lives or sustaining severe injuries in eastern Ukraine, forcing Putin to consider the unpopular move of ramping up military mobilization. With no battlefield victory in sight, Putin has reasons to entertain a diplomatic off-ramp.

Industry observers note that trump and Xi could press Putin to accept a set of limited but consequential steps to de-escalate the conflict. These could include an agreement between Russia and Ukraine—brokered and monitored by Washington and Beijing—to end attacks on energy installations and infrastructure, civilian targets, and commercial shipping. Trump and Xi could also jointly press Putin to refrain from actions that could broaden the war, such as penetrating NATO airspace with Russian drones, sabotaging European infrastructure, and threatening to use nuclear weapons. This pressure, combined with the allure of improving diplomatic and commercial ties to the United States, might convince Putin to relent on at least some of these challenges.

Sources indicate that trump could also use a trilateral summit to seek help extricating the United States from its war in Iran—a quagmire that has produced regional mayhem and soaring oil prices. As Tehran continues to problem maximalist demands and the war disrupts shipping through the straits of Hormuz and Bab el Mandeb, Trump needs an out.

Sources indicate that neither Xi nor Putin has yet been inclined to lend a hand. China is still buying Iranian oil and providing Tehran with military intelligence and dual-use items that end up in Iranian drones and missiles, and Russia is providing satellite targeting data, munitions, advanced drone technology, and logistical support. Both Beijing and Moscow are happy to see the United States mired in a conflict that is exacerbating divisions within the American electorate and fracturing NATO.

In a recent development, as a major energy exporter, Russia benefits from the spike in oil prices that the conflict has triggered, so pressing Putin to cease supporting Iran is likely a lost cause. But China is the world’s largest oil importer, and Beijing has a vested interest in lowering energy prices by stabilizing exports from the Middle East. Although China’s large oil reserves have buffered its economy from rising oil prices so far, those reserves have been significantly depleted. China’s crude oil imports have begun to climb again, leaving its economy exposed to high energy prices if the conflict drags on. And as the world’s largest exporter of goods, China suffers from the dampening effect high energy prices have on global growth.

Sources indicate that xi might therefore be amenable to helping Trump end the war. Trump should ask Xi to stop or at least slow the flow of Chinese dual-use items to Iran. Washington’s naval blockade and financial and commercial sanctions on Tehran have already taken a toll on Iran’s economy and military supply chains. By cutting off Chinese technology shipments to Iran, Beijing could deepen this economic isolation and help convince Tehran to negotiate an end to the conflict.

Recent findings suggest that xi could also press Iran to drop its unrealistic demands for ending the war, including that the United States withdraw its forces from the Gulf, release frozen Iranian assets, and remove economic sanctions. Washington might well be willing to offer economic relief, but only as part of postwar negotiations toward a deal that reins in Iran’s nuclear ambitions. Xi could help clear the way for those talks by urging Iran to accept credible terms for ending the immediate conflict.

Beyond working to resolve current conflicts, Trump should promote future strategic stability by pursuing arms control negotiations with Xi and Putin. Every arms control agreement negotiated between Washington and Moscow has expired; their final nuclear pact, New START, ended in February. There are currently no caps on the American and Russian strategic arsenals and no regular inspections, data exchanges, or notifications of nuclear exercises. This nuclear free-for-all is particularly dangerous given Russia’s nuclear saber rattling amid the war in Ukraine and the Kremlin’s fondness for provocations such as sending explosive-laden drones into NATO airspace.

In a recent development, in October, Trump appropriately proposed that a trilateral summit include a discussion of nuclear arms control. China has long resisted engaging in arms control talks, arguing that it should not have to limit its nuclear program when its arsenal is much smaller than that of the United States and Russia. But Beijing is rapidly expanding and modernizing its nuclear arsenal. The Pentagon has projected that China will possess more than 1,000 operational warheads by 2030, putting it in nearly the same league as the United States and Russia, which have stockpiles of roughly 1,800 operational warheads each. With the uncertain trajectory of U.S.-Chinese relations, instability on the Korean Peninsula, and China’s tense relationship with Taiwan heightening the risk of conflict in East Asia, Beijing must be part of high-level nuclear arms control discussions.

In a recent development, realistically, Trump can do little more than start this conversation and invite Xi and Putin to continue it in future trilateral negotiations led by teams of diplomats and arms control experts. In future talks, the three countries should discuss not only caps on nuclear weapons stockpiles but also military-to-military contacts, crisis management protocols, notifications of military exercises, counterproliferation, and other measures that can contribute to strategic stability.

Recent findings suggest that trump could add a host of other topics to the summit’s agenda, including trade, energy security, and AI regulation, but he should avoid a wide-ranging conversation that goes nowhere. He might, however, notch an easy win by proposing a three-way initiative in an area in which cooperation is relatively straightforward—for example, a joint medical mission to the Democratic Republic of the Congo to help fight Ebola or a joint aid operation to deliver humanitarian relief to Gaza or Yemen. A concrete, public effort along these lines would show that trilateral dialogue can yield viable cooperation.

Industry observers note that yet Trump should guard against being so eager for a win that he lets Xi and Putin take advantage of him. The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit takes place only two weeks after American voters dealt Trump and his party a historic rebuke in the U.S. midterm elections. The notoriously thin-skinned president could be tempted to make concessions to Beijing and Moscow to score a foreign policy breakthrough. He must avoid making a behind-closed-doors compromise on Ukraine that he then tries to force on Kyiv and its European supporters. Similarly, he must hold the line on Taiwan even as he seeks Xi’s help on North Korea, Ukraine, and Iran. Otherwise, Trump will leave the trilateral meeting confirming the worst fears of those who foresaw a fresh Yalta in the making. Capitulating to Xi and Putin would alienate Washington’s allies, project American weakness, and erode global deterrence.

Trump must also carefully manage the optics of a trilateral summit. Putin is an indicted war criminal who continues to prosecute a ruthless war of aggression against Ukraine. It is far too soon to let him out of the penalty box. And although Washington is right to seek a good working relationship with Beijing, it is time for Trump’s “truly great friendship” with Xi to bear fruit. Trump must approach talks with sobriety and pragmatism, seeking to demonstrate that Washington, Beijing, and Moscow can work together to help promote global peace and stability.

A summit next week will not usher in a fresh era of great-power collaboration anytime soon. It might not even yield concrete deliverables. Still, the meeting would set a valuable precedent. Simply by sitting down with Xi and Putin, Trump would begin a much-needed trilateral conversation.

Latest Update: Functional Core Workouts Are the Key to Moving Better in and Out of the Gym

💡 Key Takeaways
  • I don’t know about you, but doing core exercises is my least favorite part of workouts.
  • According to recent reports, functional training focuses on compound movements that engage multiple muscle groups simultaneously and mimic the way our bodies move during everyday activities.
  • Sources indicate that for instance, a farmer’s carry mirrors the movement of carrying grocery bags.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I don’t know about you, but doing core exercises is my least favorite part of workouts. Unfortunately, though, neglecting functional core training can make a big difference in your total-body strength, and how you move day to day.

According to recent reports, functional training focuses on compound movements that engage multiple muscle groups simultaneously and mimic the way our bodies move during everyday activities. Functionally training the core, specifically, involves strengthening the abdominal muscles that attach to the pelvis or spine.

Sources indicate that for instance, a farmer’s carry mirrors the movement of carrying grocery bags. “This is an example of ‘bracing and carrying,’ where you need to keep a tight, braced core to carry the heavy weight,” notes Corrine Carnation, CPT, a personal and group trainer at Equinox and creator of the Better You, Better Living program. Plus, a weak core can lead to poor posture and an increased risk of injury.

But the benefits extend way beyond preparing your body for real-life activities and protecting against pain or injury—keep reading for all the reasons you should do functional core movements.

In a recent development, meet the experts: Corrine Carnation, CPT, is a personal and group trainer at Equinox. Cori Ritchey, CSCS, is the fitness editor at Women's Health, as well as a certified strength and conditioning coach and group fitness instructor in Upcoming York City.

Time: 30 minutes | Equipment (optional): kettlebell, dumbbells, slam ball, resistance band, or Pilates ring | Good for: core, hips, back.

Industry observers note that instructions: Choose 5 to 6 exercises from the list below. Complete 2 to 3 sets of the indicated number of reps for each move. Aim to integrate functional core exercises into your training routine once or twice a week.

As these exercises become easier with practice, challenge yourself by increasing resistance while slightly decreasing the number of reps. For example, if 3 sets of 10 reps using bodyweight alone feels easy, try adding a weight or resistance band for 2 or 3 sets of 8 reps. By the last rep of each set, you should feel ready to stop but not completely at failure. When in doubt, start with bodyweight only, then add resistance until you feel the exercise is challenging, but doable.

According to recent reports, pro tip: Exercises aren’t one-size-fits-all, so it’s crucial to recognize when an exercise is either too challenging, too easy, or not comfortable for you. Keep in mind that every exercise can be modified if needed!

Why it rocks: The suitcase carry prepares the core for real-life activities such as carrying heavy things by your sides. It strengthens the core by making you resist the urge to bend, improving stability and balance—the added grip demand is a fun challenge, too.

1. Holding a weight in one hand, stand up tall and pull your shoulders back and down to prevent them from rolling forward. Keep your core tight and spine neutral.

2. Walk forward for 30 to 60 seconds while maintaining a strong grip and upright posture.

3. Set the weight down. That's 1 rep.

4. Turn around and pick the weight up again, this time with your left hand. Complete 4 reps on each side.

Why it rocks: The halo exercise improves shoulder mobility and stability while strengthening your core. Moving the weight around your head causes a perturbation (or distracting force) to your body, forcing you to stabilize using your core. This particular halo variation has the added benefit of enhancing upper-body strength, targeting the shoulders, back, and arms.

Recent findings suggest that 1. Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, holding one dumbbell in front of your chest with both hands and elbows bent at 90 degrees.

In a recent development, 2. Slowly circle the dumbbell around your head, moving it clockwise from ear to ear, elbows hugging in.

3. Return to start and repeat the movement counterclockwise. That's 1 rep.

Recent findings suggest that why it rocks: Have you ever worried about straining your back when picking something up or twisting? This move strengthens the core, improves stability, and builds rotational strength to protect your body during these movements.

1. Sit on the floor with your knees bent and upper body leaned back until abs are engaged (aim for a 45-degree angle relative to the floor). Hold a slam ball or dumbbell close to your chest with your elbows bent.

2. Keeping your arms slightly bent, twist your torso to the left and slam the ball on the floor next to your left hip.

In a recent development, 3. Twist your torso through center to the right and slam the ball on the floor near your right hip. That's 1 rep.

4. Continue alternating for a total of 10 to 12 reps.

Industry observers note that why it rocks: The overhead slam exercise requires you to stabilize your body as you lift and forcefully throw the ball down to the floor. It also strengthens your shoulders, arms, and upper back while improving explosive power and coordination.

1. Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart, a soft bend in knees, and core engaged, while holding a slam ball at your chest with both hands.

2. Rise up tall on your toes and extend your arms overhead holding the slam ball.

Recent findings suggest that 3. Bend at your hips (hinging forward slightly) and slam the ball on the floor directly in front of you. Exhale as you throw the ball down toward the floor with force. Be careful not to arch your back.

Recent findings suggest that 4. Catch the ball on the bounce while lowering back into the squat position. That's 1 rep.

Why it rocks: The wood chop exercise helps strengthen your core by working your abs and obliques, which can boost your twisting power and stability, building strength and coordination.

It has been revealed that 1. Start in a half-kneeling position with your left leg forward and your right leg back, both bent at 90 degrees, holding a dumbbell in front of your chest.

Industry observers note that 2. With your arms straight, torso upright, and hips facing forward, swiftly lower the weight diagonally across your body to the right hip while twisting to the right. Then, raise the weight to upper left diagonal while twisting to the left. That's 1 rep.

Recent findings suggest that 3. Complete 10 reps, then repeat on the other side.

Sources indicate that why it rocks: Keeping your lower back and head flush with the floor while your limbs shift weight will engage your deep core stabilizers. Being able to lift your legs and arms from this position is essential for a healthy spine.

In a recent development, 1. Lie faceup holding one dumbbell horizontally in front of your chest with both hands. Lift legs to a tabletop position with your knees over hips, your lower back glued to the floor, and your core engaged.

It has been revealed that 2. Keeping one leg at a 90-degree angle, lower the other to tap your heel to the floor. As your leg lowers, reach your arms above your head to lower the weight toward the floor behind your head.

3. Engage your core to lift both your arms and leg back to start, then repeat on the opposite side. That's 1 rep.

Why it rocks: This exercise recruits your abdominal muscles to maintain balance and stability. A resistance band offers an added challenge for the core and lower body.

1. Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart and your hands on your hips or relaxed at your sides. (Optional: Place a resistance band around the arches of both feet.).

2. Balancing on one leg, draw one knee up toward your chest, hold for 1 second, then return it to the floor.

Sources indicate that 3. Repeat on the opposite side, alternating for 30 seconds. That’s 1 rep.

Industry observers note that why it rocks: Planks help you build the strength to push yourself up from the floor, which is important for many day-to-day activities. Adding the knee drive challenges your upper body and core to stabilize, improving your balance and coordination with uneven movements.

1. Start in a high plank position with your right foot lifted slightly up off the floor.

2. Exhale and pull your right knee toward your chest while rounding the spine to bring your nose toward your knee.

3. With control, reverse movement to return to plank position with right foot lifted. That's 1 rep.

4. Complete 10 to 12 reps on each side.

Why it rocks: This exercise challenges you to sit up and lie down without using your hands, which requires strong core muscles. You can do it with a Pilates ring, a ball, or no equipment at all.

1. Lie faceup with your legs slightly bent, heels on floor, and arms extended straight above your head. (Optional: Place a mini resistance band around your wrists for an added challenge.).

Industry observers note that 2. Engage your core and draw your belly button in as you slowly begin to curl your spine off the mat one vertebra at a time. Roll up to an upright seated position while keeping biceps by the ears and arms reaching to the ceiling.

It has been revealed that 3. Once you reach the upright position, gradually reverse the movement by slowly rolling back down to the lying position. That's 1 rep.

Industry observers note that why it rocks: This exercise targets the glutes and core, the muscles needed to lift your hips. It's great for anyone who sits a lot, as it both strengthens and mobilizes the hips.

Sources indicate that 1. Lie faceup with knees bent and feet planted shoulder-width apart on the floor. Place your arms on the floor by your sides or for an added challenge, extend arms above with your hands directly above your shoulders and your palms facing in.

2. Engage your core as you press up into a glute bridge with your knees, hips, and shoulders in alignment, and hold this position.

It has been revealed that 3. From here, raise your right leg to a 90-degree angle, keeping the stationary leg firmly on the floor and pelvis stable. Return right foot to meet left foot in starting position. That’s 1 rep.

It has been revealed that 4. Continue alternating legs with your butt lifted and complete 10 to 12 reps on each side.

It has been revealed that why it rocks: The classic side plank targets the obliques, which are essential for stability and rotation in daily activities. It also works your shoulders and hips, promoting good posture and alignment.

Sources indicate that 1. Lie on your right side with your legs bent, your right elbow directly under your shoulder, and your left hand palm down.

Industry observers note that 2. Lift your hips off the mat, extending your legs to form a straight line from your head to heels.

Sources indicate that 3. Hold the position for 30 seconds, then repeat on the opposite side. That’s 1 rep.

According to recent reports, why it rocks: It's similar to the suitcase carry, but levels up the move a bit by testing your stabilization, as you have to stay upright even though the weight is trying to pull you down. Plus, it boosts your grip strength.

Recent findings suggest that 1. Stand up straight with feet shoulder-width apart and dumbbell in left hand.

According to recent reports, 2. Extend your right arm out to the side at a 45-degree angle from your body.

Sources indicate that 3. Slowly lift your left leg up until knee is at hip height.

Recent findings suggest that 4. Then, with control, lower your leg down to the floor. Repeat with right leg. That's 1 rep.

It has been revealed that 5. Complete 10 to 12 reps, then switch the dumbbell to your right hand.

According to recent reports, why it rocks: It targets your obliques, but also challenges your other core muscles in a more uncommon position. Additionally, it works your spinal mobility.

Sources indicate that 1. Kneel on left knee with toes pointed to the right, and right foot planted firmly to the side of body, holding a kettlebell in right hand.

Sources indicate that 2. Rack the kettlebell at chest, then lift it overhead, keeping eyes on the weight.

According to recent reports, 3. Slowly lower body down until left hand reaches the floor, then continue lowering until elbow and forearm reach the floor.

4. Reverse the movement with control and return to start. That's 1 rep.

It has been revealed that why it rocks: It's important to train rotation because we're constantly rotating in real life. Plank hip dips strengthen the obliques and stabilize the spine.

1. Start in a forearm plank position with elbows under shoulders and knees, hips, and torso in a straight line.

According to recent reports, 2. Drop right hip toward the floor, then return to center.

3. Immediately drop the left hip toward the floor.

According to recent reports, 4. Continue alternating for 45 seconds.

Why it rocks: This move is one of the best for training functional power, and it demands stabilization from your core.

Sources indicate that 1. Stand with feet slightly wider than hip-width apart. Hold a kettlebell in front of your body with both hands, arms straight.

2. With a slight bend in the knees and a flat back, hinge at the hips and swing the kettlebell back through the legs. Use that momentum to stand and swing the kettlebell out in front of your body, up to shoulder height.

3. Thrust the hips forward and engage the glutes and core as you stand up straight. When the kettlebell hits shoulder height, the knees should be straight and glutes contracted in a full hip extension.

Sources indicate that 4. Allow the kettlebell to swing back down through the legs, while hinging at the hips. That's 1 rep.

The best functional core workouts include bodyweight and resistance exercises that challenge the core in different positions and directions. Your core is not one-dimensional, so it’s crucial to strengthen your body through movements that involve twisting, bending, and stabilizing in all directions. For example, a traditional situp only engages the core in a single plane of motion, but a workout with a Russian twist (for rotational movement), lateral side bends (for side-to-side movement), and plank variations (for multidirectional stability) ensures you are hitting your core muscles from all angles.

Carnation notes the importance of first activating your core before jumping right into a workout. To do so, she recommends the following: “Act as if someone is about to throw a basketball at your stomach.” It might sound odd, but this cue can be really effective in helping you tighten and brace your core to get ready for impact. It’s best to practice this abdominal bracing technique before going into more advanced exercises in order to ensure your core is engaged and ready for action, Carnation claims.

Latest Update: Japan’s Defense Lessons From Ukraine and the Middle East

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

Since taking office in October 2025, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has been busy reforming Japan’s defense policy. Her government is revising the National Security Strategy, National Defense Strategy, and Defense Buildup Program to prepare for an era of heightened instability and growing uncertainty over U.S. engagement in the region. Notably, Tokyo raised defense and other security-related spending to approximately 1.8 percent of GDP in the 2025-2026fiscal year, up from around 1 percent in 2022. In April, Japan also revised its defense transfer policy with the aim of promoting exports of weapons and nonlethal military equipment.

According to recent reports, expanding Japan’s defense production capacity has been a central focus of these reforms. In its budget request for the 2027 fiscal year, the Japanese Defense Ministry singles out domestic military production as a critical element of deterrence. This reflects growing concerns that Japan may need to sustain military operations in a protracted, high-intensity conflict. In an analysis of the U.S.-Israel war against Iran that was published in August, the Defense Ministry explicitly recognizes the need to maintain adequate production capacity in peacetime—and to be ready to rapidly scale up weapons production in the event of a conflict.

Sources indicate that since taking office in October 2025, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has been busy reforming Japan’s defense policy. Her government is revising the National Security Strategy, National Defense Strategy, and Defense Buildup Program to prepare for an era of heightened instability and growing uncertainty over U.S. engagement in the region. Notably, Tokyo raised defense and other security-related spending to approximately 1.8 percent of GDP in the 2025-2026fiscal year, up from around 1 percent in 2022. In April, Japan also revised its defense transfer policy with the aim of promoting exports of weapons and nonlethal military equipment.

Industry observers note that expanding Japan’s defense production capacity has been a central focus of these reforms. In its budget request for the 2027 fiscal year, the Japanese Defense Ministry singles out domestic military production as a critical element of deterrence. This reflects growing concerns that Japan may need to sustain military operations in a protracted, high-intensity conflict. In an analysis of the U.S.-Israel war against Iran that was published in August, the Defense Ministry explicitly recognizes the need to maintain adequate production capacity in peacetime—and to be ready to rapidly scale up weapons production in the event of a conflict.

Sources indicate that japan’s focus on production capacity reflects a change in the way that military planners think about deterrence. Russia’s yearslong war against Ukraine and the ongoing conflict in the Middle East have demonstrated the prolonged, high-intensity, resource-draining nature of modern warfare. Some analysts now expect a potential conflict over Taiwan to play out in similar ways, rather than the quick, decisive campaign that many experts had long assumed as their base case.

NATO frames deterrence around three elements: capability (does a state have the weapons to defend itself?), credibility (would it actually use them?), and communication (does the adversary understand what it would be up against?). In a long, high-intensity conflict, each of these three pillars is increasingly shaped by production capacity.

In a recent development, production capacity affects the availability of the weapons needed for military operations both in preparation during peacetime and during an ongoing war. Recent conflicts have underlined two aspects of replenishment capability: the replacement rate (whether weapons output keeps pace with consumption in the battlespace) and the cost-to-kill ratio (how much a defensive weapon costs compared to the offensive threat that it counters).

In terms of credibility, a longer conflict is not just about the willingness to use force but also the willingness to sustain it for the duration of the conflict. The durability of public and private investment signals whether a state can support production throughout a prolonged conflict.

In terms of communication, an adversary’s calculation—and hence the deterrent effect—is affected by the signal sent by investing political and financial capital in defense production capacity.

It has been revealed that viewed through this framework, recent announcements by the Japanese government and reports on the forthcoming reforms show how production capacity relates to the three pillars of deterrence. To upgrade capability, Tokyo has indicated that it will accelerate support for domestic industry. To this end, the Japanese government is planning to release a upcoming defense industrial base strategy, likely to include new subsidies to support defense firms’ production capacity. One plan is to extend an existing scheme to the acquisition and maintenance of production facilities for ammunition and other critical supplies necessary for sustained combat capability. Through greater governmental support, Tokyo aims to establish spare defense production capacity that could sustain protracted and high-intensity warfare.

According to recent reports, to enhance credibility—by demonstrating willingness not just to spend now but also to keep spending in the future—Tokyo is working to bolster the domestic defense investment landscape. Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi has urged Japanese financial institutions to provide investment and loans to grow the domestic defense sector, and lenders are responding.

Sources indicate that in May, the Development Bank of Japan, a state-owned institution, eased its restrictions on financing domestic arms manufacturers. Private banks are also increasing their involvement in the sector. MUFG Bank, one of Japan’s largest private-sector banks, is reportedly planning to establish criteria for lending to defense-related companies after having previously been cautious. These measures normalize defense-related investments in peacetime, but they do not guarantee the financial sector’s commitment to invest in case of a longer conflict.

According to recent reports, in April, the Defense Ministry stated that Japan must not allow an adversary to believe that prolonging a conflict would ensure the success of an invasion, emphasizing the importance of stockpiling and domestic production. Koizumi has made the connection between defense production and deterrence increasingly explicit. Economy, Trade and Industry Minister Ryosei Akazawa has also been explicit about investing in the industrial base for dual-use goods in order to strengthen Japan’s ability to sustain military operations.

In terms of communicating deterrence, Tokyo is matching these efforts with political signaling that its upcoming defense-industrial posture is a long-term change that’s here to stay.

Recent findings suggest that there are still two major gaps in Japan’s production planning for a potential conflict. First—despite these initiatives—Japan is still struggling to ramp up defense production. According to the Defense Ministry’s assessments, insufficient parts production is likely to continue limiting the operational availability of military equipment, particularly aircraft, for the Japanese Self-Defense Forces.

According to recent reports, this means that Japan is still struggling to meet peacetime demand, let alone the surge in production that a protracted conflict would require. Tokyo is considering government-owned, contractor-operated facilities as a means to enable rapid defense production increases when needed, but the feasibility and potential scale of such agreements remain unclear. This problem is exacerbated by the absence of a legal framework that would allow the government to compel manufacturers to sustain operations in wartime, raising fundamental questions about Tokyo’s ability to translate expanded capacity into wartime output.

Second, Japan’s defense supply chain remains vulnerable. It is extensive and stretched thin, including around 1,100 manufacturers involved in the production of fighter jets, 1,300 for tanks, and 8,300 for destroyers. Despite Tokyo’s efforts to enhance its defense capability, protecting this extensive network remains challenging. In many cases, it is difficult to find alternative suppliers for specialized component materials or specific manufacturing processes. Consequently, disruption to any part of the supply chain could affect the stable supply and maintenance of equipment.

In a recent development, strengthening supply-chain resilience, particularly with regard to small and medium suppliers, is crucial to ensuring a stable supply of equipment. Tokyo is considering dispersing, hardening, and placing military facilities underground, but these discussions do not apply to industrial suppliers. Increasing supply-chain redundancy—both domestically and with Japan’s strategic partners—is also critical.

Industry observers note that in this respect, the deal with Australia for upgraded Mogami-class frigates, as well as discussions with Indonesia on transferring used Asagiri-class destroyers there, include cooperation on maintenance. Foreign-based maintenance facilities for Japanese-built platforms could, over time, provide additional repair capacity outside Japan.

The revision of Japan’s three national strategic documents and the Defense Industry Policy is expected to be concluded next month. The policies set out in these documents will determine the course of Japan’s defense industrial policy in the years to come. If production capacity in a protracted conflict is now part of Tokyo’s deterrence calculations, then the test for the strategy documents to be released in December will be whether they move beyond only peacetime capacity. This would entail granting the government the authority to direct production during wartime and planning how civilian manufacturers, particularly in dual-use sectors, could contribute to a wartime surge. Alongside these policies, effective strategic communication to shape an adversary’s expectations about the duration and likely outcome of a conflict will be key to strengthening deterrence.

Jumpei Ishimaru is a research analyst in the Japan program at the International Institute for Strategic Studies.
